title: Commentators: Wang Bi, Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming
bigQuestion: How did commentators turn old classics into new philosophy, and why can the same line support such different readings?

story.title: Seven Days Before the Bamboo
story.kicker: A young scholar stares at bamboo for seven days trying to find its principle, and falls ill.
paragraphs: The story comes from Wang Yangming himself, as his students recorded it in a book known in English as Instructions for Practical Living. When he was young, in the late 1400s, Wang was a devoted reader of Zhu Xi. Zhu Xi had taught that learning begins with the investigation of things.

Wang and a friend decided to take the teaching literally. Every thing, Zhu Xi said, has its principle. So they sat before the bamboo in a courtyard and set themselves to investigate it until they grasped its principle. The friend lasted three days before he fell ill from the strain.

Wang kept going. He stared at the bamboo, day after day, thinking as hard as he could. On the seventh day he too fell ill. He found nothing. Years later he told his students that he had come to think the effort was aimed in the wrong direction.

Scholars point out that the young men had misread Zhu Xi, who never asked anyone to stare at one plant. But the story became famous for another reason. It marks the start of Wang's own path. He would come to argue that principle is found in the mind itself, and that knowing and acting are one. The same classic line would be read two very different ways.
story.think: What went wrong in the bamboo experiment? Was it a failure of effort, of method, or of the teaching itself?

lessons.title: Thinking Through Notes
lessons.mainIdea: For two thousand years, many major Chinese thinkers did their philosophy by writing commentaries on the classics.
reading: Open a traditional Chinese edition of the Analects and you will see large characters for the text and small characters for notes packed between the lines. The notes are the *commentary*. Some editions carry several layers: an early commentary, a later subcommentary, and notes on both. Readers met the classics through these layers.

In Europe, philosophers often wrote new treatises under their own names. In China, many thinkers built new ideas by explaining old texts. A commentator could say something bold while presenting it as the true meaning of Confucius or Laozi. Scholars call this the *hermeneutic* tradition: the art of interpreting texts.

This means that the history of Chinese philosophy is partly a history of readings. When you read Zhu Xi, you read Zhu Xi reading the Analects. When you read Wang Bi, you read Wang Bi reading the Daodejing. To understand a later thinker, you ask what text they were explaining and what they changed.

words.d: notes that explain a classic text line by line
notes that explain an earlier commentary
the study and art of interpreting texts
a long formal essay presenting one's own argument

look.title: Layers on a Page
look.text: A page of a traditional edition: one line of the Analects in large characters. Beneath it, in small characters, He Yan's collected notes from the 200s CE. Beside those, a later scholar's notes explaining He Yan. A reader in 1600 reads all three together.
look.prompt: How would reading these layers together change what a reader takes the line to mean? What would be lost by reading only the bare text?

check.q: What is a subcommentary?
check.why: A subcommentary adds a layer of explanation on top of a commentary.

check.q: Why did many Chinese thinkers write commentaries rather than treatises?
choices: They could build new ideas while explaining honored texts
They could not write long works
check.why: Commentary let thinkers develop ideas as the meaning of the classics.

check.q: What is hermeneutics?
choices: The art and study of interpreting texts
check.why: Hermeneutics is the study of interpretation.

lessons.title: He Yan Collects the Analects Notes
lessons.mainIdea: He Yan's collected commentary of the 200s CE gathered earlier notes on the Analects and became the standard reading for centuries.
reading: He Yan, who died in 249 CE, was a scholar and official of the Wei state. With others, he compiled the Collected Explanations of the Analects, the Lunyu jijie. It gathered notes from earlier Han and Wei scholars, adding his own. It is the oldest complete Analects commentary to survive.

A collected commentary is a kind of *anthology*: it gathers voices. Readers could see several explanations of one line side by side. For about nine hundred years, until Zhu Xi's notes replaced it in the exam system, He Yan's collection was the main way scholars read the Analects.

He Yan was also linked to a new movement of thought in his time, often called Xuanxue, "Profound Learning" or "Learning of the Mysterious." Its thinkers read the Laozi, the Zhuangzi and the Book of Changes alongside Confucius. They asked about being and nonbeing. Wang Bi was its youngest star.

words.d: a Wei scholar (d. 249 CE) who compiled the Collected Explanations of the Analects
a book that gathers pieces or voices from many sources
"Profound Learning"; a third-century movement that read Daoist texts with the Confucian classics

check.q: What is He Yan's Lunyu jijie?
choices: A commentary on the Mencius only

check.why: The Collected Explanations of the Analects gathers earlier notes.

check.q: What replaced He Yan's collection as the main exam reading of the Analects?
check.why: Zhu Xi's notes became the exam standard later.

check.q: What did Xuanxue thinkers read alongside Confucius?
choices: The Laozi, the Zhuangzi and the Book of Changes

lessons.title: Wang Bi and Nothingness
lessons.mainIdea: Wang Bi (226–249) read the Daodejing as teaching that nonbeing is the root of all being, and his commentary became the standard reading.
reading: Wang Bi died at 23. In that short life he wrote commentaries on the Daodejing and the Book of Changes that are still read today. His text of the Daodejing became one of the main received versions. Much of what readers know as the standard Daodejing passed through his hands.

Wang Bi stressed *wu*, nothingness or nonbeing. For him, the Dao has no form and no name. Because it is nothing in particular, it can be the root of every particular thing. He read chapter 11's empty hub and chapter 40's "being comes from nonbeing" in this light. This view is often called "valuing nonbeing."

A famous anecdote in the Shishuo xinyu shows his balance. Someone asked why Confucius never spoke of nonbeing while Laozi spoke of it all the time. Wang Bi is said to have answered that Confucius embodied nonbeing, so he did not need to speak of it; Laozi had not fully embodied it, so he talked about it. The answer honors both sages.

words.d: a scholar (226–249) whose Daodejing commentary became standard
nothingness or nonbeing; for Wang Bi, the root of all things
a short story about a real person
A New Account of Tales of the World, a fifth-century collection of anecdotes

look.title: Why Confucius Did Not Speak of Nonbeing
look.text: Asked why Confucius never discussed nonbeing while Laozi spoke of it constantly, Wang Bi answered that the sage Confucius embodied nonbeing and so had no need to speak of it, while Laozi, not yet one with it, kept speaking of what he lacked.
look.cite: Shishuo xinyu (A New Account of Tales of the World), ch. 4, compiled by Liu Yiqing, 5th century; paraphrased for this course
look.prompt: How does Wang Bi's answer honor both Confucius and Laozi? What does it suggest about how he saw the two traditions?

check.q: What did Wang Bi teach is the root of all being?
check.why: Wang Bi stressed nonbeing as the root of every particular thing.

check.q: Which texts did Wang Bi write commentaries on?
choices: The Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean
The Daodejing and the Book of Changes
check.why: His commentaries on the Laozi and the Changes are still read.

check.q: In the Shishuo xinyu anecdote, why does Wang Bi say Confucius did not speak of nonbeing?
choices: Confucius embodied it and had no need to
Confucius did not believe in it

check.why: Wang Bi said the sage embodied nonbeing, so he did not talk about it.

sections.title: Zhu Xi and the Investigation of Things

lessons.title: Principle and Vital Stuff
lessons.mainIdea: Zhu Xi (1130–1200) taught that everything is made of principle (li 理) and vital energy (qi), and that the principle in each thing can be understood.
reading: Zhu Xi was the great organizer of what English writers call Neo-Confucianism, a revival of Confucian thought in the Song dynasty. He answered Buddhist and Daoist ideas with a full account of the world built from Confucian classics. His teachers included thinkers of the Cheng brothers' school.

Two terms are central. *Li 理*, principle, is the pattern or reason that makes a thing what it is and what it should be. It is a different word and character from li 禮, ritual. *Qi* is the vital stuff or energy that everything is made of. Every thing has both: principle gives the pattern, qi gives the form.

For Zhu Xi, human nature is principle, and so it is good, as Mencius said. But each person's qi can be clear or cloudy, which is why people act badly. Learning clears the cloud. This let Zhu Xi explain both Mencius's good nature and the plain fact that people often do wrong.

words.d: an English name for the revival of Confucian philosophy from the Song dynasty on
principle; the pattern that makes a thing what it is; not the same as li 禮, ritual
vital energy or stuff that all things are made of
the Song dynasty scholar (1130–1200) whose commentaries shaped Confucian learning for centuries

look.title: Two Words Spelled Li
look.text: li 禮: ritual, propriety, the proper forms of conduct (Analects 12.1). li 理: principle, the pattern in things (Zhu Xi). Same English spelling, different characters, different meanings.
look.prompt: Write one sentence using each term correctly. Why must a reader watch for the character when both are spelled li?

check.q: What does li 理 mean in Zhu Xi's philosophy?
check.why: Li 理 is principle; li 禮 is ritual.

check.q: How did Zhu Xi explain why people with good nature still do wrong?
check.why: Nature as principle is good; cloudy qi explains bad action.

check.q: What is Neo-Confucianism?
choices: The Song-era revival of Confucian philosophy
check.why: Neo-Confucianism names the revival led by thinkers such as Zhu Xi.

lessons.title: Investigating Things
lessons.mainIdea: Zhu Xi read the Great Learning's phrase gewu as "investigating things," a patient study of principle in the world and in books.
reading: The Great Learning is a short text that Zhu Xi made one of the Four Books. It lists steps: investigating things, extending knowledge, making the will sincere, rectifying the mind, cultivating the self, ordering the family, governing the state, bringing peace to the world. The first step is *gewu*.

Zhu Xi read gewu as "investigating things": reaching out to things and studying their principle. He thought the text had lost a passage explaining this, so he wrote a short supplement in its place. In his reading, you study one thing today and another tomorrow. Over time, understanding suddenly connects.

Zhu Xi mostly meant studying the classics, history and human affairs, not staring at plants. His method was patient and gradual. Readers praise it as disciplined learning. Critics said it split knowing from the mind and made learning endless. Wang Yangming's bamboo story comes from this debate.

words.d: a short classic text, one of the Four Books, listing steps from investigating things to world peace
"investigating things" (Zhu Xi) or "rectifying things" (Wang Yangming); the first step in the Great Learning
an added section meant to fill a gap

look.title: The Eight Steps
look.text: The ancients who wished to bring peace to the world first ordered their states; to order their states they first ordered their families; to do that they cultivated themselves; to cultivate themselves they rectified their minds, made their wills sincere and extended their knowledge; and extending knowledge lies in investigating things.
look.cite: Great Learning (Daxue), opening section, paraphrased for this course; compare Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1861
look.prompt: Put the steps in order from inner to outer. Why might a commentator's reading of the first step change everything after it?

check.q: What is the first step in the Great Learning's list?
check.why: The chain ends in the investigation of things.

check.q: What did Zhu Xi add to the Great Learning?
choices: A new chapter on the Dao
A supplement explaining the investigation of things
check.why: He thought a passage was lost and wrote a short supplement.

check.q: What did critics say about Zhu Xi's method?
choices: It split knowing from the mind and made learning endless
check.why: Critics like Wang Yangming thought it sent learners outward endlessly.

lessons.title: The Four Books and the Exams
lessons.mainIdea: Zhu Xi's commentaries on the Four Books became the official standard for China's civil service exams from 1313 to 1905.
reading: Zhu Xi grouped the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean as the Four Books. He published them together with his commentaries in 1190. He meant them as a path for learners: start with the Great Learning, then the Analects, the Mencius, and the Doctrine of the Mean.

After his death, his reputation rose. In 1313 the Yuan dynasty made his commentaries the standard for the civil service exams. For nearly six hundred years, until the exams ended in 1905, students across China memorized the Four Books through Zhu Xi's eyes. Korea's Joseon dynasty also made his school its orthodoxy.

The exams opened office to men of many backgrounds, but they excluded women entirely, and few poor families could pay for years of study. Critics, then and later, said the system turned learning into rote memorizing of one approved reading. Defenders praised its fairness compared with birth. Historians describe both sides.

words.d: the officially approved teaching or reading
the state tests used to choose officials, based on the classics
a short classic (Zhongyong), one of the Four Books, about balance and sincerity

check.q: Which four texts make up the Four Books?
choices: Four books of the Book of Songs
Analects, Mencius, Great Learning, Doctrine of the Mean
check.why: Zhu Xi grouped the Analects, Mencius, Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean.

check.q: When did Zhu Xi's commentaries become the exam standard?
check.why: The Yuan dynasty adopted them in 1313.

lessons.title: Enlightenment in Exile
lessons.mainIdea: Wang Yangming (1472–1529) came to believe, during exile in Guizhou in 1508, that principle is found in the mind itself.
reading: Wang Yangming, named Wang Shouren, was a scholar, official and general of the Ming dynasty. In 1506 he angered a powerful court eunuch and was beaten and sent to a remote post at Longchang, in Guizhou, in the southwest. There, according to his own account and his students, he had a sudden insight in 1508.

He came to think that the mind already holds principle. There is no need to seek it outside in things. Scholars summarize his view as "the mind is principle." This echoed the earlier thinker Lu Jiuyuan, a rival of Zhu Xi. So the later movement is often called the School of Mind, set against Zhu Xi's School of Principle.

The insight changed Wang's reading of gewu. Zhu Xi read ge as "reaching" things. Wang read it as "rectifying": setting right the intentions of the mind as it meets things. The same two characters now pointed inward. The Great Learning had not changed, but its first step had turned around.

words.d: a Ming scholar, official and general (1472–1529) who taught that the mind is principle
the line of Neo-Confucian thought, linked to Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming, that finds principle in the mind
a sudden, clear understanding

look.title: One Phrase, Two Directions
look.text: Great Learning: "extending knowledge lies in gewu." Zhu Xi: gewu = reach out to things and investigate their principle. Wang Yangming: gewu = rectify the mind's intentions as it meets things.
look.prompt: Draw an arrow for each reading: which way does learning move? What would a student do differently each morning under each reading?

check.q: Where did Wang Yangming have his insight in 1508?
choices: Longchang, in Guizhou, while in exile
check.why: He was sent to a remote post at Longchang in Guizhou.

check.q: How did Wang Yangming read gewu?
check.why: Wang read ge as rectify, turning the step inward.

check.q: Which earlier thinker is linked with Wang in the School of Mind?
check.why: Lu Jiuyuan, Zhu Xi's rival, is linked with Wang Yangming.

lessons.title: Knowing and Acting Are One
lessons.mainIdea: Wang Yangming taught the unity of knowing and acting: to truly know something good is already to act on it.
reading: A student once told Wang Yangming that people know they should honor their parents but often fail to do it. So knowing and acting must be two things. Wang disagreed. In Instructions for Practical Living, he says such people do not yet truly know. Real knowing already includes doing.

His example was simple. Seeing a lovely color belongs to knowing. Loving it belongs to acting. But you love it the moment you see it. You do not see it first and then decide to love it. In the same way, true moral knowledge moves a person at once. This teaching is called the *unity of knowledge and action*.

Wang also taught *liangzhi*, "innate knowing of the good," a term he took from Mencius 7A.15. Everyone, he said, has this inner knowing. The task is to extend it into every act. Critics warned that trusting the mind could lead to careless study. Admirers said it made learning live.

words.d: Wang Yangming's teaching that true knowing already includes acting (zhixing heyi)
innate knowing of the good; a term from Mencius 7A.15 central to Wang Yangming
Chuanxilu, the record of Wang Yangming's teachings kept by his students

look.title: Seeing and Loving a Color
look.text: Wang Yangming said that seeing a beautiful color is a matter of knowing, and loving it is a matter of acting; but one loves it as soon as one sees it, not by seeing first and then deciding to love. True knowledge of filial piety is like this.
look.cite: Wang Yangming, Instructions for Practical Living (Chuanxilu), part 1, paraphrased for this course; compare trans. Wing-tsit Chan, 1963
look.prompt: Does the color example fit moral knowledge? Think of a time someone knew what was right and still did not do it. How would Wang explain it?

check.q: What did Wang Yangming say about people who know they should honor parents but do not?
choices: They do not yet truly know
check.why: For Wang, real knowing already includes doing.

check.q: Where does the term liangzhi come from?
check.why: Wang took liangzhi, innate knowing, from the Mencius.

check.q: What example did Wang use to show knowing and acting are one?
choices: Seeing and loving a beautiful color
check.why: One loves a lovely color the moment one sees it.

lessons.title: Two Readings Across East Asia
lessons.mainIdea: The Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming readings spread across Korea and Japan, where scholars defended, blended and challenged them.
reading: In Korea, the Joseon court made Zhu Xi's school its orthodoxy. Scholars such as Yi Hwang, known as Toegye (1501–1570), and Yi I, known as Yulgok (1536–1584), debated how principle and qi relate in human feelings. Their letters are major works of philosophy. Wang Yangming's teaching was often viewed with suspicion there.

In Japan, Zhu Xi's school gained official support under the Tokugawa shogunate. Wang Yangming's teaching, called Yomeigaku, also found strong followers, some of them activists who stressed action. Other Japanese scholars, like Ito Jinsai, tried to go back behind both to the Analects and Mencius themselves.

Vietnamese scholars also studied Zhu Xi's commentaries for exams. The debate between principle in things and principle in the mind became a shared East Asian conversation. Today scholars in Seoul, Kyoto, Taipei and Beijing still study it. This course names these readers and does not rank them.

words.d: Yi Hwang (1501–1570), a leading Korean scholar of Zhu Xi's school
the Japanese name for Wang Yangming's school of thought
the Japanese shogunate (1603–1868) that supported Zhu Xi's school

lessons.title: Reading a Commentary Critically
lessons.mainIdea: A careful reader asks of any commentary what text it explains, what question it answers and what it adds.
reading: Every commentary answers questions of its own time. Wang Bi wrote when thinkers were debating being and nonbeing. Zhu Xi wrote when Buddhism offered a strong account of mind and world, and Confucians wanted a full answer. Wang Yangming wrote when Zhu Xi's readings had become an exam routine.

So you can read a commentary with four questions. What text and line is it explaining? What *problem* of its time is it answering? What new terms does it bring in, such as nonbeing or principle? And what does it change or add to the plain text? These questions keep you from mixing the classic with its reader.

This is not a way of dismissing commentators. Many readers value them as the best guides to the classics. Many traditions of practice also live through commentary. Knowing a reading's history lets you respect it and see it clearly. It also helps you see your own reading as one more in a long line.

words.d: in reading history, the question a thinker was trying to answer
putting something in the wrong time, such as reading a later idea into an earlier text
reading that asks questions about a text's claims, purpose and context

look.title: Four Questions for a Commentary

look.prompt: Answer the four questions for Wang Bi's reading. Then try them on Zhu Xi's reading of gewu.
